Abstract 12

We used wastewater monitoring data to evaluate the impact of public health policies and 13

interventions on the spread of COVID-19 among a university population. We first evaluated the 14

correlation between incident, reported COVID-19 cases and wastewater SARS-CoV-2 RNA 15

concentrations and observed changes to the correlation over time. Using a difference-in- 16

differences approach, we evaluated the association between university COVID-19 policy 17

changes and levels of SARS-CoV-2 RNA concentrations in wastewater. Policy changes 18

associated with a significant change in campus wastewater SARS-CoV-2 RNA concentrations 19

included changes to face covering recommendations, indoor gathering bans, and routine 20

surveillance testing requirements and availability. We did not observe changes in SARS-CoV-2 21

RNA concentrations associated with other policy changes. The work presented herein 22

demonstrates how longitudinal wastewater monitoring of viruses may be used for causal 23

inference such as policy impact evaluation, especially at small geographic scales. 24

1.0 Introduction 26

Nonpharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) are actions that aim to reduce the spread of an 27

infectious disease in a community—especially when the community has little immunity to the 28

pathogen or a vaccine is not yet available.1 Examples of NPIs implemented widely in the United 29

States at the start of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic include face mask 30

mandates, stay-at-home orders, non-essential business closures, and large gathering bans.2 31

Although the implementation of NPIs intended to benefit communities by flattening the epidemic 32

curve—that is by reducing the peak number of cases and burden on the health care system— 33

the implementation of NPIs also led to negative economic consequences and tolls on social 34

well-being.3–5 Governments and institutional leadership are tasked with balancing public health, 35

social well-being, and economic prospects in the face of epidemics. Evidence-based knowledge 36

can help policymakers and leaders make better-informed decisions in dire situations. 37

Following the initial wave of the pandemic, several studies empirically assessed the impact of 38

NPIs on health-related outcomes. The findings of these studies suggest that NPIs reduced the 39

spread of severe acute respiratory disease syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) virus, with 40

school and workplace closures, business restrictions, large gathering bans, and mask mandates 41

among the most impactful NPIs.6–10 A review of the various methodologies used by these 42

studies found that around half analyzed raw outcome data and half analyzed computed 43

outcome data (i.e., raw outcome data was used to compute another outcome).11 The most 44

common raw outcomes analyzed were clinical surveillance reports (e.g., confirmed cases or 45

deaths) and human mobility (e.g., tracking of mobile phones).11 The most common computed 46

outcomes analyzed were COVID-19 growth rate and effective reproduction number.11 47

Although clinical surveillance and mobile phone tracking are the most common sources of data 48

used to evaluate NPIs, these data are not without biases and limitations. Counts of confirmed 49

cases depend on clinical testing capacity and clinical testing rates, and deaths that occur 50

outside of hospitals may be underreported.6–8,10,11 Furthermore, clinical testing behaviors have 51

drastically changed with the availability of self-administered antigen tests which are not reported 52

to health departments.12 Although mobility data through tracking of mobile phones is unaffected 53

by changes in clinical testing, these data are biased towards individuals who opt into location 54

history sharing and may not be a reliable proxy for SARS-CoV-2 transmission dynamics.13,14 55

Wastewater monitoring, which has gained heightened attention since the start of the COVID-19 56

pandemic, is a promising data source because it does not suffer some of the limitations of 57

clinical surveillance and mobility data for epidemiological inference. 58

Wastewater monitoring refers to analyzing a sample of wastewater, which represents a pooled 59

biological sample of the contributing population, for concentrations of infectious disease 60

markers. Wastewater monitoring data capture contributions from both symptomatic and 61

asymptomatic individuals and are not influenced by clinical testing availability or clinical test- 62

seeking behaviors.15 Studies have reported that concentrations of SARS-CoV-2 RNA in 63

wastewater solids are correlated with laboratory-confirmed incident COVID-19 cases—although 64

this correlation has changed since the widespread availability of self-administered antigen 65

tests.16–19 Several studies also demonstrated that wastewater monitoring can be used at 66

geographic scales smaller than a sewershed (i.e., the population serviced by a wastewater 67

treatment plant) to gain insight about COVID-19 incidence.20–32 A potential use case for 68

wastewater monitoring at subsewershed scales is to assess public health policies. 69

The World Health Organization particularly suggests sampling at finer spatial scales when using 70

wastewater monitoring data to inform targeted control interventions.15 Previous studies 71

evaluating NPIs using clinical surveillance or mobility data were mostly conducted at national or 72

subnational scales, and few of these studies investigated variation in the impact of NPIs on 73

health-related outcomes among subpopulations.11 NPIs may be more or less impactful in a 74

specific subpopulation compared to the general population (e.g., due to different interaction 75

patterns) or public health goals may differ among subpopulations (e.g., universities aim to 76

maximize on-campus activity).33 Wastewater monitoring data may be well-suited to objectively 77

assess NPIs, particularly among subpopulations and despite low clinical testing rates. 78

In this study, we evaluate the potential use case of wastewater monitoring data to empirically 79

assess the impact of NPIs on the spread of COVID-19 among a university population. We begin 80

by assessing the correlation between wastewater concentrations of SARS-CoV-2 RNA and 81

incident, reported COVID-19 cases at Stanford University and evaluate changes to this 82

correlation over time. Next, we evaluate the association between policies implemented at 83

Stanford University and changes in wastewater concentrations of SARS-CoV-2 RNA using a 84

difference-in-differences (DiD) approach. DiD is a quasi-experimental design commonly used in 85

econometrics—although it was first used in 1854 by John Snow for epidemiologic purposes— 86

that aims to assess the impact of an intervention on an outcome but without the use of 87

randomization.34–36 DiD designs have been used by several previous studies to evaluate the 88

causal effects of COVID-19 policies on clinical or mobility outcomes.37–44 89

2.1 Wastewater monitoring data 95

We used wastewater monitoring data from the Codiga Resource Recovery Center (CR2C) and 96

the Palo Alto Regional Water Quality Control Plant (RWQCP) for this analysis. CR2C is a pilot 97

scale wastewater treatment facility that services a portion of the Stanford University campus 98

(California, USA) including academic buildings and student and faculty housing (Figure S1 in 99

the Supporting Information (SI)).45,46 CR2C services approximately 10,000 people with an 100

estimated daily flow of approximately 0.5 million gallons of wastewater each day.20,46 CR2C is a 101

subsewershed of the sewershed serviced by RWQCP which is operated by the City of Palo Alto 102

(California, USA). RWQCP services approximately 236,000 people and treats approximately 20 103

million gallons of wastewater each day for Los Altos, Los Altos Hills, Mountain View, Palo Alto, 104

Stanford University, and the East Palo Alto Sanitary District (Figure S1 in the SI).47 105

Prospective, longitudinal wastewater sampling from CR2C and RWQCP began July 2021 and 106

October 2020, respectively, and is currently ongoing. Six samples per week are collected from 107

CR2C; seven samples per week are collected from RWQCP. Sampling from CR2C was 108

temporarily reduced to two samples per week between 1 November 2022 and 31 December 109

2022. Details about sampling and processing methods, including quality assurance and quality 110

control metrics, are registered in protocols.io48–50 and have been described previously by Wolfe 111

et al.51 and Boehm et al.52 A brief description is provided in the SI (Text S1). 112

For this analysis, we used concentrations of the SARS-CoV-2 RNA N gene in wastewater 113

settled solids in gene copies (gc) per gram (g) dry weight (gc/g), both unnormalized (N) and 114

normalized by pepper mild mottle virus (PMMoV) RNA concentrations in wastewater settled 115

solids in gc/g (N/PMMoV). The N gene target is located near the frequently used N2 assay 116

target,53 and we have confirmed no mutation in the target over the course of the pandemic.19 117

2.4 Correlation analysis 146

Incident COVID-19 cases within the CR2C subsewershed were reported daily while between 2– 147

6 wastewater samples per week were collected and analyzed from CR2C during the analysis 148

period. Clinical case surveillance data may contain reporting biases on weekends. To compare 149

the two time series, we calculated weekly average N concentrations, N/PMMoV concentrations, 150

and incident COVID-19 cases for each epidemiological week (i.e., Sunday through Saturday). 151

Neither raw nor log10-transformed weekly average N or N/PMMoV concentrations from CR2C 152

are normally distributed (Shapiro-Wilk normality test, p < 0.01), so we used Kendall’s tau 153

correlation to test the null hypothesis that weekly average wastewater SARS-CoV-2 RNA 154

concentrations and weekly average incident COVID-19 cases in the CR2C subsewershed are 155

not temporally correlated. We tested this null hypothesis using both unnormalized (N) and 156

normalized (N/PMMoV) wastewater concentrations. We used the KendallTauB function from the 157

DescTools R package to compute the 95% confidence interval for each tau estimate.59 158

We further conducted three subgroup correlation analyses. First, we grouped the data by 159

whether wastewater sample or clinical specimen collection occurred during the academic year 160

(autumn, winter, or spring quarter) or nonacademic year (summer quarter). We used the date 161

halfway between the last day of classes of the previous quarter and first day of classes of the 162

following quarter to define the start and end of quarters.60 Second, we grouped the data by 163

whether wastewater sample or clinical specimen collection occurred before or after the 164

requirement for laboratory-based surveillance testing was suspended for vaccinated and 165

boosted students (7 April 2022) (Table 1). The laboratory-based surveillance testing program 166

required fully vaccinated students to test once a week (twice a week for unvaccinated students) 167

and therefore intended to capture both symptomatic and asymptomatic cases through routine 168

testing. Third, we grouped the data by whether wastewater sample or clinical specimen 169

2.5 Policy impact evaluation 178

We used PMMoV-normalized wastewater concentrations for the remainder of the analysis as 179

the correlation between incident COVID-19 cases and wastewater SARS-CoV-2 RNA 180

concentrations were similar using N and N/PMMoV, and a mass balance model suggests the 181

N/PMMoV ratio should scale with incidence rate.55 To assess the association between campus 182

COVID-19 policies and changes in N/PMMoV measurements at CR2C, we used a difference-in- 183

differences (DiD) approach. For the DiD design, we assumed that policies went into effect at 184

midnight on the date of implementation (day = 0). We defined the pre-treatment period as the 14 185

days before a policy was implemented (days -14 to -1) and the post-treatment period as the 14 186

reasonable comparison group for the CR2C subsewershed. With the exception of the East Palo 190

Alto Sanitary District, RWQCP services cities in Santa Clara County which is the same county 191

that Stanford University is located in. Santa Clara County entered the least restrictive “Yellow 192

4.0 Conclusions 384

We assessed the correlation between wastewater concentrations of SARS-CoV-2 RNA and 385

incident, reported COVID-19 cases at a university and evaluated changes to this correlation 386

over time. Consistent with other studies, we provide evidence that the correlation between 387

wastewater SARS-CoV-2 RNA concentrations and incident COVID-19 cases has changed over 388

time. We further investigated the use of longitudinal wastewater monitoring data for policy 389

impact evaluation. Using a DiD approach, we observed that most dates on which changes to 390

campus COVID-19 policies occurred were not associated with a significant change in 391

wastewater SARS-CoV-2 RNA concentrations on campus. However, we did not expect to 392

observe a significant change in wastewater SARS-CoV-2 RNA concentrations after all policy 393

change dates, particularly those dates on which existing policies were phased out. The work 394

presented herein demonstrates how longitudinal wastewater monitoring of viruses may be used 395

for causal inference such as policy impact evaluation, especially at small geographic scales. 396
